title: Trump Administration Ends Duration of Status for International Students, Imposing Four-Year Cap That Could Cost US Economy $145 Billion
excerpt: The new DHS rule replaces decades-old flexibility with fixed visa periods, forcing 1.2 million international students to apply for extensions and threatening to drive talent to Canada, Australia, and the UK.
body:
• DHS published a final rule on July 17 replacing "duration of status" with a four-year maximum stay for F-1 student and J-1 exchange visitor visas, effective 60 days from Federal Register publication.
  • A National Academies-commissioned study estimates the rule could cost the US economy $72–145 billion annually over ten years — more than 22 times DHS’s own cost estimate.
  • The rule halves the post-OPT grace period from 60 to 30 days and requires USCIS approval for school transfers, field-of-study changes, and extensions — creating new fees of $300–$2,400 per student.
  • India and China are among the most affected countries, with roughly half of surveyed international PhD students saying they would not have come to the US under the new framework.

What Changed

The Department of Homeland Security on July 17 finalized a regulation that eliminates "duration of status," a nearly 50-year-old policy that allowed international students and exchange visitors to remain in the United States for as long as they were enrolled in an approved program. Under the new framework, F-1 student visas and J-1 exchange visitor visas carry a fixed admission period capped at four years.

Students who need additional time — and more than half of first-time bachelor’s degree recipients take longer than four years, while the median doctoral student spends nearly six years on a dissertation — must file a formal Extension of Stay application with US Citizenship and Immigration Services. The rule takes effect 60 days after publication in the Federal Register, subject to congressional review.

“This is forcing international students to pay an extra $300 to $500 in filing fees, plus another $1,900 in premium processing if they want a response prior to five months.”

— Danielle Goldman, Co-founder and CEO, Build Talent Labs

The Economic Stakes

The populations affected are among the most productive contributors to the American economy. International students at US universities contributed $42.9 billion and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year, according to NAFSA. Education-related travel service exports were valued at $53.58 billion in 2024 by the Bureau of Economic Analysis.

A study commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine estimated that the rule will create annual losses of $72 billion to $145 billion over ten years — more than 22 times DHS’s own cumulative ten-year cost projection of $3.3 billion. The researchers compared the economic impact to “the disappearance of the entire economy of the state of Delaware.”

The Georgetown University Center for Security and Emerging Technology found that more than half of US-employed computer scientists with graduate degrees were born abroad, and nearly 70 percent of current students in US computer science programs are international. The National Science Foundation reported that international PhD recipients earned 60 percent of all engineering doctoral degrees and 54 percent of all mathematics and statistics doctoral degrees awarded in the United States.

What This Means for Indian Students

India sends the second-largest contingent of international students to the United States, and the rule hits particularly hard on the graduate students and STEM researchers who form the pipeline for the H-1B visa workforce. The regulation restricts the use of Day 1 Curricular Practical Training for students pursuing a second degree at the same academic level — a common pathway for Indian students seeking specialized credentials.

The fixed four-year window is especially problematic for PhD students in engineering and sciences, fields where Indian students are heavily concentrated. A survey of roughly 1,000 current international PhD students and postdoctoral fellows found that approximately half said they “definitely” or “probably” would not have come to the United States if they had known duration of status would be eliminated.

The regulation also requires USCIS approval for school transfers, changes in field of study, and any modification to a student’s program — decisions that were previously handled by university international student advisors in real time through DHS’s Student and Exchange Visitor Information System.

Academic and Medical Training at Risk

The International Medical Graduate Taskforce stated that it would be “impossible” for physicians to complete many graduate medical education programs within four years, including general surgery, geriatrics, and cardiology. International physicians account for nearly 25 percent of the US physician workforce and frequently serve in medically underserved areas. The Health Resources and Services Administration projects a shortfall of 141,160 physicians by 2038.

Sixteen state attorneys general submitted formal comments opposing the proposed rule, citing direct financial impacts to public universities. California estimated $230 million in annual payments from international students to public institutions, while New Jersey calculated $217 million. NAFSA estimated that continued restrictions could cost the US economy $7 billion in revenue and more than 60,000 jobs.

What’s Next

The rule faces a congressional review period and will likely draw legal challenges from universities and immigration advocacy organizations. The Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration noted that international students are increasingly choosing Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom over the United States, a trend the new regulation is expected to accelerate. Germany has also emerged as a leading alternative, offering free tuition at public universities and faster pathways to work permits.

For Indian students currently in the United States or planning to enroll, immigration attorneys recommend consulting with university international student offices immediately about how the transition period will affect their specific program timelines and any pending transfers or extensions.
